facts: Janzour is made up of eight major areas, including Janzour As-Souq, Al-Garbiyah, Ash-Sharqiya, Al-Wasat, Al-Gheiran, An-Njila, As-Sayad and Alhachan.

facts: US private oil investment in Libya was about $5 billion (replacement value), with about $500 million in annual profits to US corporations.

events.what: Anti-Jewish pogrom in Tripolitania under British military occupation; more than 140 Jews killed (including 36 children) and hundreds injured over 5-7 November 1945, with synagogues looted and homes and businesses destroyed.
Wave of anti-Jewish rioting hit Aleppo, Cairo and, most severely, Tripoli, on the anniversary of the Balfour Declaration.
Anti-Jewish rioters killed 12 Jews and destroyed 280 Jewish homes; Jewish self-defence units fought back.

facts: At least 550 Libyan Muslims were arrested for suspected involvement and tried by British military courts.

Five synagogues in Tripoli and four in provincial towns were destroyed; over 1,000 Jewish residences and commercial buildings were plundered in Tripoli.
In 1941 about 25% of Tripoli's population was Jewish and 44 synagogues were maintained in the city.
From 1948 to 1951, 30,972 Jews immigrated to Israel.

facts: The official name was the Great Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya from 2 March 1977 until the fall of Tripoli on 20 August 2011.
The word 'Al-Uzma' (Great) was reportedly added after the April 1986 US raid, on the grounds that Libya had defied great powers.
The People's Congresses were said to be organised in about 30,000 communes of roughly 100 people each.

summary: A 1987 Library of Congress country study describes the history of Arab migration into Libya, the Arabization of Berbers, tribal life, and the spread of Arab culture. It gives no specific places, events or people in or near Tripoli.
facts: Arab migrations beginning in the seventh century imposed Islam and Arabic; Bani Hilal and Bani Salim tribes invaded Cyrenaica and later Tripolitania in the eleventh century.
Arab arrivals in North Africa during the first two migrations did not exceed 700,000, and did not constitute more than 10 percent of the population of 6 or 7 million in the twelfth century.
Traditional Arab life was still predominant in the countryside at Libyan independence in 1951; petroleum wealth and urban migration later made inroads.
By the 1980s tribal life appeared to be fast becoming a thing of the past, as the revolutionary government discouraged nomadism.

summary: A 1987 Library of Congress country study describes Libya's agriculture: its share of GDP fell from about 26 percent in 1958 to 2 percent in 1978 as oil wealth grew, and food imports rose sharply. It also covers the 1981-85 plan and the GMMR water project, with no places in or near Tripoli named.
facts: In 1958 agriculture supplied over 26 percent of GDP and Libya exported food; by 1962 it was 9 percent and by 1978 2 percent.
In 1977 the value of food imports was more than 37 times greater than in 1958.
Over 94 percent of Libya's land was agriculturally useless wasteland.
The 1981-85 development plan made agriculture a cornerstone and funded the GMMR project to bring water from the Sarir and Al Kufrah desert oasis aquifers.
In 1984 agriculture accounted for about 3.5 percent of GDP and Libya imported over 1 million metric tons of cereals.
About 70 percent of Libya's food needs were met by imports in the mid-1980s.
quote: Despite the greater attention to agriculture, however, in 1984 this sector only accounted for about 3.5 percent of GDP, and Libya still imported over 1 million metric tons of cereals

summary: A December 1970 cable from the U.S. Embassy in Tripoli argues that Libya's success in forcing higher oil prices exposed Western dependence on oil and that the U.S. and allies need to study options. It concerns oil economics and OPEC strategy rather than specific places or events in Tripoli.

The cable expects Libya to make additional revenue demands within six to nine months.
An OPEC meeting at Caracas was expected the following week.
quote: Extent of dependence by Western industrial societies upon oil as a source of energy has been exposed, and practicality of controlling supply as means of exerting pressure for raising price of oil has been dramatically demonstrated.

summary: A 1970 State Department memo, forwarded to Kissinger, assesses how North African governments might react to a U.S. decision on an Israeli arms request. It says Libya is the most exposed U.S. position because of oil interests, the American community, and the ongoing Wheelus liquidation.

summary: A 1986 US embassy cable from Rabat reports on a meeting with King Hassan II of Morocco, where US officials pressed for Moroccan cooperation against Libya's Qadhafi. It covers Morocco's fears of Libyan subversion and the Oujda Accord, with no details about Tripoli itself.

The US wanted US-Moroccan cooperation against Libya to be the centrepiece of talks during Hassan's upcoming US visit.

summary: A Wikipedia background article on the 20-28 August 2011 Battle of Tripoli, describing the uprising, rebel advance, and fighting at Bab al-Aziziya, Abu Salim, Tajura, Mitiga, Janzur, Green Square and other districts. It is a secondary account, not an eyewitness source.

Rebels from Zawiya entered Janzur and then passed into the western suburbs.
Rebels breached the compound, took a gate and stormed Gaddafi's personal residence.

Rebels secured Qasr bin Ghashir, a village near Tripoli International Airport.
NLA forces took the last remaining loyalist base in Salaheddin after seven hours of fighting.

summary: A February 1977 CIA intelligence memorandum assesses Qadhafi's plan to reshape Libya's government into a "people's democracy" with a civilian structure that would sideline the Revolutionary Command Council and the military. It describes his motives after the 1975 Muhayshi coup attempt, the planned tribal-based political structure, and reactions among officers, the middle class and the business community. It names no Tripoli sites.

places.name: Sabhah
places.detail: Qadhafi's small desert hometown where the new government was to be inaugurated and where the Qadhafa tribe is centered.

events.what: Coup attempt engineered by council member Umar Muhayshi and a small clique of army officers, which led to wide dissatisfaction and an investigation of the conspiracy.

people.role: Libyan leader who plans to create a 'people's democracy' civilian government

people.role: Commander-in-Chief of the Libyan armed forces

people.name: Fidel Castro
people.role: Foreign notable invited to the new government's inauguration

facts: The plan calls for a national people's congress, a secretary general and a cabinet, with a president (presumably Qadhafi) elected by the congress.
Qadhafi has responded to unrest by upgrading police and paramilitary forces at the expense of the army and replacing suspected disloyal officers with kinsmen and tribesmen from his home region.
The memorandum says the Revolutionary Command Council has theoretically ruled Libya since 1969.
Four Council members remained active at the time of the memorandum.
quote: Qadhafi has been on the defensive since 1975, when a coup attempt engineered by council member Umar Muhayshi and a small clique of army officers brought to the surface wide-ranging dissatisfaction with Qadhafi's one-man rule.

summary: A September 2, 1969 NSC memo from Harold Saunders assesses the coup that brought Colonel Sa'ad al-Din Abu-Shuawayrib and a Revolutionary Command Council to power in Libya, and notes concern to keep Wheelus Base insulated from events. It gives no specific Tripoli street or site detail beyond Wheelus.

places.name: Wheelus Base
places.detail: The Royal Libyan Air Force was based there and depended entirely on US logistical support; the US wanted to keep it insulated from the coup.

events.what: A group of young military officers staged a coup, proclaimed the 'Arab Republic of Libya' and set up a Revolutionary Command Council, while the King was in Turkey and the Crown Prince renounced his prerogatives.

facts: The coup was dated around September 1, 1969, and the memo was written as of the end of Monday, September 1.
The new government's five-point statement said it would be socialist, seek solidarity with the third world, and be based on the Koran.
The King, aged 80, was in Turkey at the time of the coup.
Abu-Shuawayrib, aged 34, had attended US military schools including the Command and General Staff Officer Course in 1964-65.

links.why: The memo states the Royal Libyan Air Force was based at Wheelus and depended entirely on US logistical support.

quote: Since Americans do not seem to be in danger, the main contingencies we have to think about involve Wheelus Base.

summary: A 1987 Library of Congress country study describes traditional Libyan attitudes toward women and men, and how women's roles varied by age, education and residence (beduin, village, urban). It has no specific places, events or sites in or near Tripoli.
facts: Until the discovery of petroleum, and to a lesser degree until the 1969 revolution, conservative attitudes and values about women dominated Libyan society.
Girls were typically married in their early teens to men considerably older, and a woman gained status in her husband's family mainly by producing sons.
Urban women walked in the street discreetly in veiled pairs and avoided public gathering places and social contact with men, while rural women moved more freely.
The document notes that girls' secondary school enrolment and young women's access to modern-sector jobs had begun only during the 1960s.
quote: Like all Arabs, Libyans valued men more highly than women.

summary: A Pakistani newspaper series describes about 2,700 Pakistanis recruited as watchmen for Libya who were instead moved to desert and military camps, given guerrilla training, and in some cases sent abroad. The camps named include Jang Zur and Ghaylan near Tripoli, and sites in the Sahara and near Benghazi.

places.name: Jang Zur military camp
places.detail: Military camp on the Mediterranean shore, formerly part of the port customs zone, where the first Pakistani recruits were lodged after arriving in Tripoli on 26 January 1981.

places.name: Ghaylan camp (Bu Ghaylan / Jetty Sulayman)
places.detail: Pakistani recruits' camp about 10-20 km from Tripoli, next to Jang Zur, holding about 500 Pakistanis; the text also calls it Ghaylan Camp 20 km from the city.

places.name: Saba' Abril (7 April camp)
places.detail: Camp near Tripoli, translated as '7 April', holding 392 Pakistanis, about 10-20 km from the city.

places.name: Al Shuwayrif camp
places.detail: Guerrilla training camp in the Sahara about 750 km from Tripoli, described as resembling an Italian-era fort, where Pakistanis were held behind barbed wire.

places.name: Bu Ghalyan camp
places.detail: Military camp about 200 km from Al Shuwayrif in black-rock desert, where Pakistanis were moved in April 1981.

places.name: Benghazi Coast camp and Southwest Farm
places.detail: Two camps near Benghazi; Benghazi Coast was a military camp holding 102 Pakistani commandos, Southwest held 460.

places.name: Al Kufrah military site
places.detail: Military site in the Sahara near the Chad and Sudan border, holding 302 Pakistanis.

events.what: Al Murtaza Associates' first group of Pakistani recruits arrived in Tripoli and was sent to the Jang Zur military camp.
First group of about 200 Pakistanis moved to Al Shuwayrif camp, 750 km from Tripoli, where they were given military training.
100 Pakistani ex-military men were flown from Tripoli to Damascus, refused to go on to Beirut, were beaten and returned to Tripoli, then held at Ghaylan camp.
An 11-member Pakistani government delegation toured six camps and negotiated release of about 2,700 Pakistanis.

facts: Recruits were promised 120 dinars monthly as watchmen, but were moved to camps and given guerrilla training.
The Libyan government reportedly paid the Bukhari brothers 600,000 dinars, with 300,000 deposited in a Swiss bank.
The Bukhari brothers' firm was named Bridges and registered in Liberia.
Pakistani recruits were reportedly flown by United African Airlines, described as an unregistered airline used to transport troops.
Pakistani commandos were organised into companies of Infantry, Artillery, Cavalry and Signals under an organisation called al-Sa'iqah.

summary: An FBIS daily report from April 1980 covering Libya in brief: Qadhdhafi attended the arrival of the missile patrol boat Umm al-Thougoor for the Libyan navy, and a Soviet ambassador ruled out a near-term Qadhdhafi trip to Moscow. Other items cover Morocco, Israel and Lebanon with no Tripoli-specific content.

events.what: Celebrations marking the arrival of the rocket-carrying patrol boat Umm al-Thougoor, first of a batch of advanced naval vessels being delivered to the Libyan Arab Naval Forces; Qadhdhafi attended with General Army Commander Brigadier Abu Bakr Younis Jabir and the navy commander.

people.name: Mu'ammar al-Qadhdhafi
people.role: Libyan supreme commander of the armed forces and head of state

people.name: Abu Bakr Younis Jabir
people.role: Libyan General Army Commander, Brigadier

people.name: Leonid Brezhnev
people.role: Soviet President, reported at a clinic outside Moscow

facts: The patrol boat Umm al-Thougoor is the first of a batch of advanced naval vessels being delivered to the Libyan Arab Naval Forces.
The Soviet ambassador to Libya ruled out a Qadhdhafi visit to Moscow in the coming days, per Ar-Ra'y al-'Amm (Kuwait, reported via KUNA).
Reports earlier in the week said Qadhdhafi would visit Moscow as representative of the Arab Confrontation Front.
quote: the arrival of the rocket-carrying patrol boat Umm al-Thougoor, which is the first in a batch of similar advanced naval vessels which are currently being delivered to the Libyan Arab Naval Forces

summary: A Libyan Foreign Secretariat statement, broadcast on Tripoli radio, condemns a U.S.-Somali agreement granting U.S. military bases and facilities in Somalia as imperialist. The rest of the document covers Israeli and U.S. reactions to a Security Council vote and does not concern Libya.
facts: Libyan Foreign Secretariat condemned a U.S.-Somalia agreement granting U.S. military bases and facilities in Somalia, broadcast by Tripoli Voice of the Arab Homeland on 25 August 1980.
The Libyan statement said the U.S. had already secured similar bases from Oman (Qabus) and Egypt.
quote: The Foreign Secretariat of the Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriyah... expresses strong condemnation of the agreement which the Somalia regime has signed with America

summary: A February 1984 Libyan radio (JANA) report carries Qadhafi's cable calling for use of all means of war to destroy the U.S. Mediterranean fleet over Lebanon, and a commentary claiming U.S. withdrawal from Lebanon was a disguised defeat. Nothing specific to Tripoli sites or residents.

people.role: Libyan leader ('brother leader of the revolution'), sender of cable

people.name: Hafiz al-Asad

people.name: Walid Junblatt
people.role: leader of the Lebanese National Salvation Front, recipient of cable

people.name: Ronald Reagan

facts: Qadhafi's cable, broadcast by JANA on 9 Feb 1984, called for using all means of war to destroy the U.S. fleet in the Mediterranean if U.S. aggression against the Arab homeland did not stop.
JANA said copies of the cable were sent to all serving Arab rulers, the UN President and Security Council members, and the U.S. Congress.
The commentary claims the USS New Jersey shelled civilians in Lebanon, killing and wounding dozens.
quote: if the American people prove incapable of curbing the madness of actor Reagan, we must all shoulder our responsibility to future generations and the world and use all the means of war that we possess to destroy the U.S. fleet in the Mediterranean

summary: An FBIS report carries Libyan JANA texts of the Arab People's Congress emergency session held in Tripoli on 1-2 July 1982 on the Israeli invasion of Lebanon. The congress decided to send a high-level delegation representing the General People's Congress to the Soviet Union.
The congress called for a national popular committee for jihad and volunteering.

The 32nd Brigade headquarters complex in Misrata was besieged by protesters on 27 February 2011.

The article says Khamis Gaddafi was killed in fighting in Tarhuna on 29 August 2011.

summary: Qadhdhafi addressed officers and cadets at a military academy on the OAU anniversary, denouncing a French-led African alliance as neo-colonialism and calling for Egypt to return to the struggle. Foreign policy content with no Tripoli-specific site or event.

Qadhdhafi said Libya was still awaiting Egypt's reply to his Tobruk call for a meeting of the two countries' armed forces commanders to plan liberation of Sinai.

summary: A Wikipedia background article on massacres during the 1911-1912 Italo-Turkish War, covering the Sciara Sciat (Shar al-Shatt) killings of Italian troops in October 1911 and the Italian reprisal massacre of civilians in the Mechiya oasis. It is a secondary reference, not an eyewitness source.

places.name: Mechiya oasis
places.detail: Oasis where Italian troops reportedly massacred about 4,000 people over three days in reprisal in October 1911.

events.what: Ottoman forces attacked Italian troops at Sciara Sciat and reportedly massacred captured Italian soldiers (503 men, per some accounts).
Italian troops attacked the population of the Mechiya oasis in reprisal, killing about 4,000 people over three days, according to contemporary accounts.

Italian corpses at Sciara Sciat were allegedly nailed to trees with eyes and genitals mutilated, possibly in retaliation for sexual offenses against local women.

summary: A 1979 Arabic-language article by Dr Mahmud al-Salawi, reprinted by JPRS in 1980, surveys Libya's water resources and urges full use of them. It describes the Jifarah plain, Naffusah mountain, dams and aquifers around Tripoli, with few security or regime specifics.

facts: The article gives the area of the Jamahiriyah as about 175,954 hectares.

Nearly one half of the Jamahiriyah's population is concentrated in the western part of the country.
The Water Resources and Soil Authority (formerly the Secretariat of Dams and Water Resources) studies groundwater in the western part of the country.

summary: A 1981 JPRS report summarizes a Beirut weekly story saying Libya proposed an oil-for-goods barter deal with India, asking Kamani Engineering to accept oil instead of cash for an advance on a transmission contract. The story is about oil pricing and OPEC, with no Tripoli-specific content.
facts: Libya asked Kamani Engineering Corporation (Bombay) to accept oil instead of cash as advance payment for a transmission construction contract.
The contract was one of two Kamani was bidding for in Libya, combined value about 23 million dollars.
The advance payment would affect about 10 per cent of the transmission contract value.
The matter was referred to the state-owned Indian Oil Corporation for study.
Algeria proposed a similar oil-for-goods barter deal with Japan at the weekend before the report.
Libya, Algeria and Nigeria were OPEC's highest-priced producers, about eight dollars above Saudi Arabia's 32-dollar marker price.
quote: Libya has joined Algeria in proposing an oil for goods barter deal with India in a bid to counter pressure for a reduction in the official price of its crude.

facts: The colony was unified in 1934 under governor Italo Balbo and initially divided into three regions: Cyrenaica, Tripolitania and Fezzan.

facts: Libya had a population of 3.6 million in 1984.

Libya gained independence in 1951 and oil was discovered in 1957.
The 1 September 1969 coup marked the start of a period of growing government intervention in the economy.
Libya held accumulated net gold and foreign-exchange reserves of upward of US$4 billion, with oil income estimated at US$6 to 8 billion a year.

facts: The Ottoman Maghrib was divided into three regencies: Algiers, Tunis and Tripoli.

The khouloughlis were offspring of Turkish soldiers and Arab women who held high administrative posts.
Jews and moriscos were active as merchants and craftsmen in Tripoli; some moriscos were pirates.
European slaves and enslaved blacks from the Sudan were a feature of city life.

summary: Wikipedia background article on Mitiga airport in Tripoli, formerly Wheelus Air Base and Okba Ben Nafi Air Base. events.what: Airport originally built by the Royal Italian Air Force as Mellaha air base.
British 8th Army captured the airbase; US Army Air Forces began using it as a base the same month.
Renamed Wheelus Army Air Field in honour of Lieutenant Richard Wheelus, who died in a 1945 plane crash in Iran.
US Air Force left the base, which was renamed Okba Ben Nafi Air Base and used by the Libyan People's Air Force and Soviet aircraft.
Base bombed by US F-111 aircraft during Operation El Dorado Canyon, at 2 a.m.
Air base converted to a civilian airport for Tripoli and given its current name.
Colonel Ali Atiyya of the Libyan Air Force at the airport defected to anti-Gaddafi forces.
Rebels launched an assault on Mitiga as part of the battle for Tripoli, with a number of casualties.
Airport spokesman announced closure due to airstrikes during the 2019–20 Western Libya campaign.
Afriqiyah Airways Flight 209 from Sabha to Mitiga was hijacked and diverted to Malta.

facts: The base was used by the US 376th Bombardment Group (Heavy) of the 12th Air Force for B-24 missions into Italy and Germany.

One 48th TFW F-111F was lost in the 1986 raid, presumably to a SAM or AAA hit.

The Libyan base housed the LPAF headquarters and a large share of its major training facilities.

summary: A Wikipedia article describes Buq Buq, a forced labor camp in Egypt's Matrouh Governorate run by Italy in 1942 that held about 350 Libyan Jewish men, mostly from Tripoli, who built and repaired roads. It is a secondary background source, not an eyewitness account, and it describes Italian-run repression of Libyan Jews rather than events in Tripoli itself.

places.name: Buq Buq
places.detail: Forced labor camp at the Egyptian-Libyan border in Matrouh Governorate, Egypt, operated by Italy from August to November 1942.

places.name: Sidi Azaz
places.detail: Libyan labor camp from which the 350 prisoners were transferred to Buq Buq.

events.what: Camp opened at end of August 1942; prisoners built and repaired roads for Axis supply between Cyrenaica and Egypt.
Italian forces dissolved the camp and evacuated prisoners after the British victory at El Alamein; survivors were ordered back to Tripoli.
Camp population fell from 350 to just over 200 by end of October due to discharges of sick and injured laborers.

people.name: Moshe Hadad
people.role: Jewish engineer from Tripoli who served as senior prisoner overseer (capo) at Buq Buq

people.name: Rachel Simon
people.role: Historian cited on the selection process

facts: Camp held 350 Libyan Jewish men aged 18 to 45, mostly from Tripoli and surrounding area.
Camp had no permanent guard force; an Italian military doctor was the only permanent official, and the commandant of Sidi Azaz oversaw it.
Prisoners lived in tents of 4 to 8 men; malnutrition, water shortages and heavy labor caused widespread illness.
Camp was frequently bombed by the RAF in late October 1942.
In 2002 Germany accepted responsibility for imprisonment of Jews in six Libyan camps, including Buq Buq.
No trials of Italian military personnel relating to Buq Buq have taken place.

links.why: Prisoners were transferred to Buq Buq from the Libyan Sidi Azaz labor camp.
Most prisoners came from Tripoli and the surrounding area and were ordered back to Tripoli after the camp was dissolved.

quote: The labor camp at Buq Buq was a forced labor camp for Libyan Jews, operated by Italy between August and November 1942 at the Egyptian-Libyan border in Buq Buq

facts: The square was founded in the 1920s under the name Italia Square (ميدان إيطاليا).
After Libya's independence in 1951 it was named Independence Square (ميدان الاستقلال).
The last name, Martyrs' Square, was confirmed after the 17 February revolution.
Streets branching off the square include Omar al-Mukhtar, Mizran, 24 December (formerly 1 September) and Independence (formerly Amhamed al-Miqrif).
The square has a fountain depicting winged horses.
Buildings overlooking the square include the Banco di Roma building (later Republic Bank, then Umma Bank) and the former Wilaya (province) building.

quote: Inscriptions found in Egypt dating from the Old Kingdom (ca. 2700-2200 B.C.) are the earliest known recorded testimony of the Berber migration and also the earliest written documentation of Libyan history.

events.what: Prisoners rebelled in June 1996 demanding fair trials and better conditions, and security forces carried out one of the largest massacres of the Gaddafi era there.
Protests began after the arrest of lawyer Fathi Terbil, which led to demands for the regime's overthrow.
Protests grew after more than 400 people were reported killed or wounded by security forces and mercenaries.
Tripoli rose up, and the article says the capital fell within nine hours after the controlling brigade refused to fight.
Rebels entered Tripoli on 21 and 22 August, according to the article.

facts: The article says the 1996 Abu Salim prison massacre was carried out by internal security, and that the prison is not run by the Ministry of Justice.
The article says the 1996 football fans' massacre and the 2006 Benghazi demonstrations were also major episodes of repression under Gaddafi.
The article says Gaddafi and his forces were defeated in Sirte, and that he was killed there by 20 October.
The article describes the 1969 coup as the Al-Fateh revolution, and says the state name changed to the Socialist People's Libyan Arab Jamahiriya in 1977.

links.why: The article links the June 1996 prison revolt at Abu Salim to the massacre carried out there by security forces.

summary: A 1987 Library of Congress country study describes Libya's manufacturing and construction sector under Gaddafi, including industrial policy, heavy industry projects, and declines caused by the oil price fall and loss of foreign workers. facts: Before the revolution, 90 percent of Libya's manufacturing establishments were located in Benghazi or Tripoli, and 75 to 80 percent were owned by Italians.
In 1983 manufacturing contributed about 4 percent of GDP and employed an estimated 80,500 people, about 7 percent of the labour force.
The 1981-85 development plan allocated LD2.725 billion to heavy industry, 15 percent of the total.
Key heavy projects in 1981-85 plan included an ammonium/urea expansion at Marsa al Burayqah, an ethylene unit at Ras al Unuf, and an iron and steel complex at Misratah.
In 1986 construction supplied about 11 percent of GDP; construction workers fell from 371,000 to 197,000 between mid-1983 and mid-1984.
In 1975 the government reorganized the construction industry, which had about 2,000 contractors.
quote: Before the revolution, 90 percent of Libya's manufacturing establishments were located in Benghazi or Tripoli, and 75 to 80 percent of these were owned by Italians.

Typhus epidemic broke out among about 2,600 Jews from Cyrenaica held at Giado; the document says over 500 Jews were killed in the Cyrenaica blow.
Most severe post-World War II anti-Jewish violence in Arab countries; over 130 Jews, including 36 children, were killed and five synagogues in Tripoli were destroyed.
Further riots in which 15 Jews were killed and 280 Jewish homes destroyed.

facts: Italian Libya had about 40,000 Jews before the war, and the document says none remain in the country today.

Over 30,000 Libyan Jews emigrated to Israel between 1948 and Libyan independence in December 1951.
Bukbuk camp had no guards or fences, and its prisoners were released in November 1942 after Italian forces retreated.
Expelled Jews with French citizenship (about 1,600) went to Tunisia; over 400 with British citizenship were sent to Italy.

facts: The U.S. reservations concerned Algeria's policy of engaging Qadhafi in dialogue and drawing Libya into a Maghreb configuration.

facts: In November 2010 the Libyan armed forces were estimated at 76,000 personnel, plus about 40,000 People's Militia.
The Libyan army was estimated at 50,000 troops in 2009 (25,000 volunteers and 25,000 conscripts).
Khamis Gaddafi's 32nd Brigade ('Khamis Brigade') was one of the main regime protection forces.
The Libyan Navy was established in November 1962; total navy personnel were about 8,000.
The Libyan Air Force was created in 1963 and had an estimated personnel strength of 22,000 in 2005, with 13 military airbases.
The People's Militia was about 45,000 in 1987 with a mission of territorial defence.

facts: Megrahi was born in Tripoli on 1 April 1952 and was reportedly the director of the Centre for Strategic Studies in Tripoli.
Megrahi was released on compassionate grounds on 20 August 2009 and flown to Tripoli; he was discharged from hospital on 2 November 2009 and died on 20 May 2012.
Megrahi and Fhimah were held under armed house arrest in Tripoli after being indicted in November 1991.
